## Why This Is Asked

Tests understanding of admission control, per-namespace scoping, and Cosign-based image signing in CKAD-level design. It combines Deployments, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, Secrets, ValidatingWebhookConfiguration, and NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts
- ValidatingWebhookConfiguration scope by namespace label
- Cosign-based image signing and public key storage in ConfigMap
- InitContainer usage for tooling
- Secrets for registry credentials
- NetworkPolicy for webhook traffic control

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal Guard Deployment (cosign setup) - placeholder
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: guard-service
  namespace: guarded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-cosign
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache cosign && cosign version"]
      containers:
      - name: guard
        image: guard-service:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 443
```

```yaml
# Minimal WebhookConfiguration skeleton
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: image-signature-validator
webhooks:
- name: images.example.com
  clientConfig:
    service:
      name: guard-service
      namespace: guarded
      port: 443
    caBundle: <base64-ca>
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    resources: ["pods"]
    operations: ["CREATE"]
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      guard: "true"
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test for false positives/negatives and monitor webhook latency?
- What risks are introduced by admission webhooks and how would you mitigate them?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical token rotation using common CKAD primitives: InitContainer, Secrets, CronJob, and network policies in a per-namespace context.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for pre-population of credentials
- Secret storage and re-mounts on rotation
- CronJob for periodic credential refresh
- RBAC least privilege for Vault access
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton outline (not full manifests):
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: app-token
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: fetch-token
        image: curl:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "curl -sS https://vault.local/token -o /tokens/token.txt"]
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /tokens
          name: token-vol
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /tokens
          name: token-vol
      volumes:
      - name: token-vol
        emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: rotate-token
spec:
  schedule: "0 */6 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: rotator
            image: curl:latest
            command: ["sh", "-c", "curl -sS https://vault.local/token -o /secret/token.txt && kubectl create secret generic app-token --from-file=token.txt=/secret/token.txt --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -"]
            volumeMounts:
            - mountPath: /secret
              name: secret-vol
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
          - name: secret-vol
            secret:
              secretName: app-token
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test rotation in CI/CD? 
- How would you handle token revocation and long-running requests during rotation?

## Why This Is Asked
This tests end-to-end Kubernetes app design under CKAD constraints: deployments, secrets, configmaps, probes, resource budgeting, rolling updates, and autoscaling. It emphasizes practical, scalable patterns rather than theory.

## Key Concepts
- Deployments and rollout strategies
- Secrets and ConfigMaps
- Probes and health checks
- Resources and limits
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler
- StatefulSets and PVCs for Redis/PostgreSQL

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 25%
      maxSurge: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: yourrepo/api:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: db-creds
        - configMapRef:
            name: api-flags
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor Redis cache misses and cache hits?
- How would you handle DB credential rotation without downtime?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose common CKAD primitives into a cohesive, maintainable per-namespace app: InitContainer logic, ConfigMap-driven behavior, TLS handling, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer installs rendering tool and pre-processes inputs
- ConfigMap and Secret drive runtime config and secrets
- Sidecar for TLS rotation and secret refresh
- Readiness/Liveness probes for quick failure detection
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to internal endpoints

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: docs-portal
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: docs-portal
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: docs-portal
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: docs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: docs-pvc
        - name: tls-cert
          secret:
            secretName: docs-tls
      initContainers:
        - name: render-md
          image: pandoc/pandoc:latest
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp -r /docs/* /rendered/; pandoc -f markdown -t html /docs/*.md -o /rendered/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: docs
              mountPath: /docs
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /rendered
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:stable
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle new Markdown files added at runtime?
- How would you scale this per-namespace deployment with multiple replicas?

## Code Example

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dns-audit
  namespace: example
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dns-audit
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dns-audit

      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: alpine:3.18

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to design a secure, idempotent one-off data migration using Kubernetes Jobs, PVCs, and ConfigMaps with proper lifecycle controls.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes Jobs for one-off tasks
- PVC mounting for data access
- ConfigMap-driven script execution
- TTL cleanup and backoff handling
- Non-root execution and capability dropping
- Minimal RBAC with ServiceAccount

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: migrate-50k
  namespace: data-migration
spec:
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600
  backoffLimit: 2
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: migration-sa
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
      - name: migration
        image: python:3.11-slim
        command:
        - python
        - /scripts/migrate.py
        - --src
        - /data/src
        - --dst
        - /data/dst
        - --limit
        - "50000"
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        volumeMounts:
        - name: scripts
          mountPath: /scripts
          readOnly: true
        - name: src-data
          mountPath: /data/src
        - name: dst-data
          mountPath: /data/dst
      volumes:
      - name: scripts
        configMap:
          name: migrate-scripts
      - name: src-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: db-src
      - name: dst-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: db-dst
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Validation Steps
1. Verify ConfigMap contains the migration script: `kubectl get configmap migrate-scripts -n data-migration -o yaml`
2. Check PVCs are bound: `kubectl get pvc -n data-migration`
3. Validate ServiceAccount exists: `kubectl get serviceaccount migration-sa -n data-migration`
4. Test job creation: `kubectl apply -f migration-job.yaml`
5. Monitor progress: `kubectl get jobs -n data-migration -w`
6. Check pod logs: `kubectl logs job/migrate-50k -n data-migration`
7. Verify data migration completion through database queries

## Rollback Steps
1. Delete the job: `kubectl delete job migrate-50k -n data-migration`
2. Check for any partial data migration: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM target_table` in destination database
3. If partial migration occurred, either:
   - Rerun the job (script should be idempotent)
   - Manually clean destination data and rerun
4. Review logs for issues: `kubectl logs -l job-name=migrate-50k -n data-migration`
5. Verify source data integrity if migration failed

## Security Considerations
- Non-root execution prevents privilege escalation
- Dropped capabilities minimize attack surface
- Minimal RBAC reduces blast radius
- Read-only root filesystem prevents unauthorized writes
- Dedicated ServiceAccount isolates permissions

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to reason about per-namespace security controls, init workflows, and practical use of ConfigMaps/Secrets with network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for prep tasks and tooling installation
- Image scanning with Trivy in-cluster
- Per-namespace heartbeat and audit via ConfigMap
- Secrets for registry credentials and policy ConfigMaps
- NetworkPolicy restricting egress to vulnerability DB

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the image-scan guard
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-scan-guard
  namespace: TARGET_NS
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: image-scan-guard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-scan-guard
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl ca-certificates && mkdir -p /logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: guard
        image: busybox:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: registry-creds
        - configMapRef:
            name: scan-policy
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: image-scan-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale this to large clusters with many namespaces? 
- How would you handle false positives and performance impact during pod startup?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: Deployments, ConfigMaps, resources, probes, and autoscaling with verification.

## Key Concepts
- Deployment, ConfigMap, resources, probes, HPA
- Rollout verification, kubectl, metrics-server
- Safe rollout strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: web-env
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "128Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this for a multi-tenant cluster? 
- What changes if the app uses a sidecar log collector?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD patterns: watch resources in a namespace, ConfigMap/Secret usage, PVC-backed logs, InitContainer tooling, readiness/liveness, and a restrictive NetworkPolicy. It exercises multi-resource coordination and security boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped controllers and watches
- ConfigMap updates and digest semantics
- Secrets for credentials and secure API calls
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Probes for reliability
- PVC-based logging
- Namespace NetworkPolicy egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton: Deployment (audit-logger), ConfigMap (audit-digest), Secret (audit-token), PVC (audit-logs), NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: audit-logger
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-logger
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: audit-logger
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: logger
        image: your-registry/audit-logger:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        env:
        - name: AUDIT_ENDPOINT
          value: "https://audit-portal.example/api/v1/heartbeat"
        - name: AUDIT_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-token
              key: token
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/ready"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: audit-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you RBAC-scopes affect the watch and updates to the ConfigMap?
- What would you monitor to handle digest collisions or out-of-order heartbeats?
- How would you test this in a CI pipeline?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
CKAD requires practical mastery of node-scoped components, DaemonSets, hostPath volumes, and real-world log shipping patterns.

## Key Concepts
- DaemonSet on each node with hostPath volumes
- Log tailing with tail -F and sidecar shipping
- ConfigMap-driven batching (BATCH_SIZE)
- NodeSelector to target workers
- Readiness/Liveness probes and lifecycle (preStop)
- Resource requests/limits and rollback strategy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-collector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-collector
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-collector
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/os: linux
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: busybox:stable
        command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log | /usr/local/bin/shipper --endpoint http://log-portal:5000/api/v1/logs --batch-size $(BUS_BATCH)" ]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 15
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 30
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["sh","-c","sleep 10"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log
          type: Directory
``` 

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test under burst log loads and verify end-to-end delivery? 
- How would you rollback a DaemonSet rollout if a regression is found?
